claims.text: Operations management is the business function that turns inputs - materials, people, machines, money and time - into finished goods or services, and its task is to combine those resources so output meets customer demand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managing resources effectively means producing the output customers want while wasting as little of the inputs as possible: the right quantity, the right quality and the right timing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Poorly managed resources cause failure at three points: not enough output, so customers whose demand is unmet may buy elsewhere; wrong quality, so reputation and repeat sales suffer; or wasteful production, so costs rise and profit margins shrink.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Effective resource use is measured through efficiency: a business that produces the same output with fewer inputs, or more output with the same inputs, has lowered its cost of production, which tends to widen its profit margin or give it room to cut price and win sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Production measures the volume of output a business produces in a given time, such as bricks, loaves or haircuts per week.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Productivity measures output per unit of input - most often output per worker in a given time - so it is a ratio rather than a total.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Production and productivity can move in different directions: taking on more workers raises total production while leaving output per worker - productivity - unchanged or even lower, so production alone does not show how well resources are used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Efficiency is the relationship between the inputs used and the output produced: production is efficient when it achieves the most output from the fewest inputs, or the required output at the lowest cost of resources.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can raise productivity by automation and technology, which let machines handle repetitive stages faster and more consistently than hand work, and by improving labour skills through training, which lets workers produce more or better output in the same time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Raising efficiency tends to lower the cost of each unit produced, because the same total input cost is spread over more output; that saving can widen the profit margin or let the business cut its price and win sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Efficiency gains carry risks that can undo them: automation needs heavy investment that may never be recovered if demand falls, and it can demotivate workers who fear redundancy, so improved labour skills is often the slower but lower-risk route.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Inventories are the stocks of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods that a business holds to support its production and its sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses hold raw material stocks so that production continues when a supplier is late or a delivery is unreliable; a production line that stops for want of one input stops paying for all the others.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses hold finished goods so they can meet customer demand immediately, because a customer who finds the shelf empty may buy from a rival instead, and a business that can supply at once tends to keep that customer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Holding inventories carries costs: storage space, insurance, the risk of damage, theft and deterioration, and money tied up in stock that cannot be spent elsewhere; holding less stock frees cash but increases the risk of running short.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Lean production is an approach that cuts every form of waste from the production process - wasted materials, wasted time, idle stock and unnecessary work - so that only the resources that add value remain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Just-in-time inventory control is a lean technique in which materials arrive from suppliers only as the production line needs them and finished goods are produced only as orders arrive, so inventories are close to zero.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Kaizen is a lean technique of continuous small improvements suggested and carried out by the workers themselves, which raises efficiency because the people closest to the process see its waste first and small changes add up without heavy investment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The benefits of lean production are lower inventory and storage costs, less wasted material and labour time, lower unit costs and better quality, because a process stripped of waste exposes defects instead of burying them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job production makes one item at a time, made to the customer's own specification, with work carried out by a single worker or team from start to finish.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Batch production makes a group of identical items in one run, with the line or machines reset between batches to make the next group, so it suits products made in varieties of the same design.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flow production moves the product continuously along a line of stages, each performing one operation, so it suits a single standardised product made in very large volumes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each method trades unit cost against flexibility: job production gives motivated, high-quality, custom work at the highest unit cost; batch spreads set-up costs across the run but the line waits while it is reset; flow gives the lowest unit cost on standardised output but is inflexible and a fault can stop the whole line.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing a production method depends on the nature of the product and the size of the market: one-off, customer-specific products point to job production; a range of varieties sold in moderate quantities points to batch; one standardised product in very large volumes points to flow.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: No method is the right one in the abstract: each needs weighing against the business's market, its costs and its capacity, so the recommendation should name the decisive criterion - usually the match between the order pattern and what each method does well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Technology has changed production by moving design and manufacturing onto computers - computer-aided design develops and tests products on screen, and computer-aided manufacture controls the machines that make them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New production technology tends to raise productivity and consistency while cutting waste, but it needs large investment, retraining and maintenance, and it can make workers redundant, so a business weighs the savings against those costs and human consequences.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flow production and batch production differ in whether the line stops to change over: batch production makes a group of identical items and then resets the machines for the next group, while flow production moves one standardised product continuously with no runs and no resets, so a batch run that becomes longer is still batch production while changeovers remain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Lean production and flow production answer different questions: flow production is one of three methods of organising production, suited to a single standardised product made in very large volumes, while lean production is an approach to cutting waste that can be applied under job, batch or flow production.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Just-in-time is one method of inventory control, not inventory control in general: inventory control is any policy for how much stock to hold and when to reorder, including holding a buffer stock, while just-in-time keeps stock close to zero by having materials arrive as the line needs them, which works provided suppliers are reliable and near.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
